pharm: A thiopurine antimetabolite that is converted intracellularly to thioguanine nucleotides which incorporate into DNA/RNA and inhibit purine synthesis, used for remission induction and consolidation of acute nonlymphocytic (myeloid) leukemia.
quick: Approximately 2 mg/kg of body weight orally once daily as part of leukemia induction/consolidation
Take on an empty stomach for consistent absorption; oral total daily dose, often once daily
Can cause fetal harm; avoid in pregnancy, especially first trimester
Avoid breastfeeding during therapy due to potential serious harm to the infant
Use with caution; no fixed adjustment but monitor for increased toxicity
Avoid/discontinue with liver toxicity; high risk of veno-occlusive disease
Avoid alcohol; adds to hepatotoxicity risk
CBC with platelets, liver function and clinical signs of hepatotoxicity (VOD)
summary: Thioguanine (TABLOID; 6-thioguanine, 6-TG) is an oral purine-analog antimetabolite used for remission induction and remission consolidation of acute nonlymphocytic (myeloid) leukemia, typically in combination with other agents. It is NOT recommended for maintenance therapy or long-term continuous use because of a high risk of hepatotoxicity, particularly hepatic veno-occlusive disease (sinusoidal obstruction syndrome). The usual dose is about 2 mg/kg/day. Thioguanine must be discontinued at the earliest signs of liver toxicity, hepatic tenderness, hepatomegaly, unexplained weight gain/fluid retention, or jaundice. Patients deficient in TPMT or NUDT15 are at markedly increased risk of severe, life-threatening myelosuppression and require substantial dose reduction. Myelosuppression is the dose-limiting toxicity.
indications: Remission induction and remission consolidation of acute nonlymphocytic (acute myeloid) leukemia in adults and children, generally in combination with other chemotherapeutic agents
Not recommended during maintenance therapy or similar long-term continuous treatment because of the high risk of liver toxicity (hepatic veno-occlusive disease)

Handle as a hazardous/cytotoxic drug using appropriate precautions; wash hands after handling
Compute the dose to the nearest multiple of 20 mg based on body weight and response
Discontinue at the earliest sign of hepatotoxicity (hepatic tenderness, hepatomegaly, weight gain/fluid retention, jaundice, or rising liver enzymes/bilirubin)
Do not use for routine maintenance because of cumulative hepatic veno-occlusive disease risk
moa: Thioguanine is a sulfhydryl analog of guanine that acts as an antimetabolite. After cellular uptake it is converted by hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) to thioguanylic acid (6-thioguanosine-5'-monophosphate, TGMP) and subsequent thioguanine nucleotides. These nucleotides inhibit several steps of de novo purine biosynthesis and purine interconversions, and are incorporated into DNA and RNA in place of guanine, producing strand breaks, miscoding, and cell death. The cytotoxic effect requires intracellular activation; thiopurine S-methyltransferase (TPMT) and NUDT15 govern metabolism and inactivation, so deficiency in these enzymes leads to accumulation of active thioguanine nucleotides and severe myelotoxicity.

absolute: Prior resistance to thioguanine (cross-resistance with mercaptopurine is usual, so do not switch from one to the other when resistance to the other thiopurine is documented)
relative: Pre-existing liver disease or prior hepatotoxicity
TPMT or NUDT15 deficiency (very high myelosuppression risk)
Concurrent hepatotoxic drugs or significant alcohol use
Bone marrow depression or active serious infection
monitor: Liver function tests, serum bilirubin, and clinical signs of hepatic veno-occlusive disease (tender hepatomegaly, weight gain, jaundice, ascites)
Complete blood counts with platelets for myelosuppression
TPMT/NUDT15 status in patients with severe or recurrent toxicity

preg: Thioguanine can cause fetal harm when administered to a pregnant woman and is teratogenic/embryolethal in animals; congenital abnormalities and miscarriage have been reported, particularly with first-trimester exposure. Avoid pregnancy during treatment; advise patients of the potential hazard to the fetus and recommend effective contraception. If used in pregnancy or if the patient becomes pregnant, inform the patient of the potential risk.
lact: It is not known whether thioguanine is excreted in human milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions and tumorigenicity in the breastfed infant, women should not breastfeed during thioguanine therapy.
renal: There are no specific dosing adjustments established for renal impairment, but caution is advised because reduced clearance may increase toxicity. Monitor closely for myelosuppression and adjust dose based on tolerance.
hepatic: Thioguanine is hepatotoxic, with hepatic veno-occlusive disease (sinusoidal obstruction syndrome) being the most serious concern, especially with prolonged or maintenance use. Use with great caution in patients with hepatic impairment. Discontinue thioguanine at the earliest signs of liver toxicity, including hepatic tenderness, hepatomegaly, unexplained weight gain or fluid retention, ascites, jaundice, or significant elevations in transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, or bilirubin. Monitor liver tests weekly when starting therapy and periodically thereafter.

major: Other hepatotoxic drugs (e.g., busulfan and other agents) - additive risk of hepatic veno-occlusive disease and liver injury
Myelosuppressive chemotherapy or radiation - additive bone marrow suppression
Aminosalicylates (sulfasalazine, mesalamine, olsalazine) - inhibit TPMT and increase thioguanine nucleotide levels and myelotoxicity
moderate: Live vaccines - avoid due to immunosuppression and risk of disseminated infection
Drugs affecting TPMT activity - may alter active metabolite exposure
minor: No clinically significant minor interactions specifically documented
interactions.food: Take on an empty stomach for more consistent absorption; bioavailability is incomplete and variable.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol because it adds to the risk of hepatotoxicity.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor CBC with platelets and liver chemistries (AST/ALT, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin); consider TPMT/NUDT15 genotyping or phenotyping.

serious: Hepatotoxicity, especially hepatic veno-occlusive disease (sinusoidal obstruction syndrome) presenting as hepatomegaly, weight gain, jaundice, and ascites
Severe, prolonged myelosuppression (life-threatening in TPMT/NUDT15-deficient patients)
emergency: Hepatic veno-occlusive disease / acute hepatic failure (jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, rapid weight gain/ascites)

monitoring: Complete blood counts with platelets frequently (the rapidity of marrow recovery determines tolerated dose); be alert for rapid falls in counts
Liver function tests (transaminases, alkaline phosphatase) and serum bilirubin - weekly at start of therapy, then periodically; watch for veno-occlusive disease
Clinical signs of hepatotoxicity: hepatic tenderness, hepatomegaly, unexplained weight gain/edema, ascites, jaundice - discontinue promptly if these occur
TPMT and NUDT15 status in patients with severe or recurrent myelosuppression
Serum uric acid and signs of tumor lysis during induction; signs of infection and bleeding
counsel: This medicine is used only for short courses (induction/consolidation), not for ongoing maintenance, because of serious liver risk
Report right away any yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, belly swelling or pain over the liver, or sudden weight gain - these can signal serious liver injury
Report fever, sore throat, unusual bruising or bleeding, or signs of infection promptly
Avoid alcohol and tell your doctor about all medicines, including sulfasalazine/mesalamine and other liver-affecting drugs
Avoid pregnancy and breastfeeding; use effective contraception during treatment
pk: Hematologic effects develop over days to weeks; requires intracellular conversion to active thioguanine nucleotides
Variable, incomplete oral absorption (roughly 30%); peak plasma levels within a few hours
Plasma parent drug short (about 80 minutes), but active nucleotides persist intracellularly much longer
Cytotoxic effect outlasts plasma levels due to retained DNA-incorporated nucleotides; dosed daily
Store at controlled room temperature, approximately 15-25 C, in a dry place
pearls: Hepatic veno-occlusive disease (sinusoidal obstruction syndrome) is the signature toxicity - DO NOT use thioguanine for maintenance or long-term continuous therapy
Discontinue immediately at the earliest signs of liver toxicity: hepatic tenderness, hepatomegaly, weight gain/fluid retention, ascites, or jaundice
TPMT or NUDT15 deficiency causes severe, potentially fatal myelosuppression - reduce dose substantially and test patients with marked toxicity
Cross-resistance with mercaptopurine is usual; do not substitute when resistance to one thiopurine is documented
Myelosuppression is dose-limiting - monitor CBC closely as counts can fall rapidly even after stopping
missed: Thioguanine is given as part of a defined induction/consolidation regimen. If a scheduled dose is missed, contact the treating oncology team for guidance rather than doubling up; the dose is generally taken when remembered the same day or skipped if close to the next dose. A delayed or missed course should be rescheduled and the regimen adjusted by the prescriber, with verification of blood counts and liver tests before resuming.
overdose: Symptoms of overdose may appear immediately (nausea, vomiting, malaise) or be delayed (myelosuppression, azotemia, liver dysfunction, gastrointestinal injury). There is no known specific antidote, and thioguanine is not appreciably removed by dialysis. Management is supportive, including monitoring and treatment of myelosuppression (transfusions, infection control) and hepatic and gastrointestinal complications; the marrow effect may be dose-limiting and prolonged.
